abstract: |
  Financial risk factor time series are essential for empirical asset pricing research, yet existing factor libraries suffer from limited reproducibility, lack of modularity, and language-specific implementations. This paper presents a comprehensive, fully replicable multilingual financial risk factor library that addresses these limitations. We provide a modular framework for constructing risk factors from raw data, encompassing data acquisition, cleaning, and portfolio aggregation. The library includes both an application programming interface (API) and native implementations in Python and R, allowing researchers to work in their preferred computational environment. Our transparent, modular design enables both reproducibility and flexibility, accommodating diverse portfolio sort configurations and adjustment methodologies. By making all code and data workflows publicly available, we promote standardization and support reproducible research practices in empirical asset pricing.

## Introduction: Constructing financial risk factors {#sec-intro}

In empirical finance, a key question is which sources of systematic risk drive asset returns. Researchers address this by constructing factor returns—portfolios isolating single economic characteristics or exposures. Factor returns allow model evaluation, hypothesis testing, benchmarking, and decomposition of returns into systematic and idiosyncratic components [@fama1993; @cochrane2011; @harvey2016].

Despite their importance, no widely adopted, transparent, and accessible source standardizes factor construction. Current practice often relies on ad‑hoc publication of factor series, usually without code or detailed workflows. This limits reproducibility, comparability, and extension. Reproducible research requires transparent workflows, standardized data processing, analysis‑ready series, and modularity to vary methodological choices.^[Existing resources illustrate this gap: the French Data Library [@fama2023] provides canonical factors but no code; the Open Source Asset Pricing Project [@chen2022] focuses on replication; the global factor database [@jensen2023] is Python‑oriented. A modular, multilingual framework is still needed.]

Our project makes four contributions. First, we release a public factor library that centralizes series and workflows. Second, we provide a modular, end‑to‑end workflow for data acquisition, cleaning, variable construction, and portfolio aggregation. Third, we offer native R and Python implementations and a programmatic API for standardized data retrieval. Fourth, all code, workflows, and documentation are published to enable replication, methodological comparison, and extensibility. Together, these improve transparency, reproducibility, and comparability.

We provide two libraries — *tidyfinance* (on CRAN) and *py‑tidyfinance* that streamline data acquisition from WRDS, Compustat, and other commonly used data providers. Automated routines handle standard lagging procedures to eliminate ad‑hoc fixes. Special adjustments typical for financial data —delistings, price or volume adjustments —are embedded. 

A core focus of our project is the handling of the construction of portfolio sorts which involve many subjective choices: breakpoints, weighting, rebalancing, handling ties, and sample inclusion. Our code treats sorting as a configurable module. All choices are documented, tested and common variants (equal- or value-weighted, double sorts, quantile/percentile breaks, overlapping portfolios) are implemented.

We illustrate the full workflow in R, from raw data to factor returns, including diagnostics. Python examples in the appendix ensure parity in configuration, defaults, and outputs.

We publish a curated factor library with preprocessed time series across sorting variables, weighting schemes, and adjustments. We demonstrate how methodological choices affect factor returns to highlight empirical relevance. Finally, a programmatic API provides access to standardized series and preprocessed panels. The database supports versioning and batch retrievals. All software, workflows, and documentation are published to enable replication, sensitivity analysis, and extension, promoting standardized benchmarking and transparent empirical research.
